choices.text: Many staphylococcal strains have developed resistance to penicillin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Penicillin cannot be delivered in an oral or intravenous form

choices.label: C
choices.text: Penicillin covers only Gram-negative rods and atypical organisms

choices.label: D
choices.text: Staphylococci are intrinsically resistant to all cell wall agents

choices.label: E
choices.text: Staphylococci lack a peptidoglycan cell wall to be targeted

explanation.summary: Penicillins cover Gram-positive cocci, but many staphylococci and streptococci have developed resistance.
explanation.whyCorrect: Penicillin VK and penicillin G have Gram-positive cocci coverage that includes staphylococci and some streptococci, but many of these organisms have developed resistance to penicillin. That resistance is precisely why the antistaphylococcal penicillins nafcillin and oxacillin were developed.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Penicillin is available as both oral penicillin VK and parenteral penicillin G.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Penicillin's coverage is Gram-positive cocci, not Gram-negative rods.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Staphylococci respond to cell wall agents such as nafcillin, cefazolin, and vancomycin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Staphylococci are Gram-positive organisms with a thick peptidoglycan wall.

questions.topicName: Spectrum of Activity and Indications 1 – β-lactams and Vancomycin

questions.stem: Bacitracin is combined with other antibiotics in a triple antibiotic ointment rather than given systemically. Which of the following best explains this formulation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It becomes effective only after absorption through the skin

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is inactivated by gastric acid whenever it is swallowed whole

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is the only agent active against MRSA in open wounds

choices.label: D
choices.text: It needs a β-lactamase inhibitor before it becomes active

choices.label: E
choices.text: The combination broadens topical coverage with low toxicity

explanation.summary: Bacitracin is combined with other antibiotics topically to widen coverage while keeping systemic toxicity low.
explanation.whyCorrect: Bacitracin covers Gram-positive organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus species, and when combined with other antibiotics in an ointment it provides broad-spectrum coverage against a wider range of bacteria. This combination is particularly useful topically because of its effectiveness and low risk of systemic toxicity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bacitracin acts locally at the wound surface rather than after systemic absorption.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Gastric inactivation is not the stated reason for the topical formulation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: MRSA infections are treated with vancomycin or ceftaroline, not bacitracin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Bacitracin is not a β-lactam and needs no β-lactamase inhibitor.

questions.topicName: Spectrum of Activity and Indications 1 – β-lactams and Vancomycin

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman has a 2-day history of left flank pain, pain with urination, urinary frequency, and fever with occasional nausea. Her temperature is 37.8°C (100°F), and she has left flank percussion tenderness; the remainder of the examination is normal. Acute pyelonephritis is diagnosed and ciprofloxacin is prescribed. This drug acts on which of the following bacterial targets?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dihydropteroate synthase in the folate pathway

choices.label: C
choices.text: DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV

choices.label: D
choices.text: Penicillin-binding transpeptidases of the cell wall

choices.label: E
choices.text: The 30S subunit of the bacterial ribosome

explanation.summary: Fluoroquinolones inhibit the type II topoisomerases DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV.
explanation.whyCorrect: All fluoroquinolones do effectively the same thing: they inhibit the type II topoisomerases DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, with variable specificity within the class. Loss of these enzymes halts DNA replication and kills the organism, which is why fluoroquinolones are bactericidal. Ciprofloxacin is a standard systemic fluoroquinolone used for urinary and other infections below the diaphragm.

whyWrongByChoice.A: RNA polymerase is the target of rifamycins, not of fluoroquinolones.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Dihydropteroate synthase is the target of the folic acid synthesis inhibitors, a different drug class.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Transpeptidases are inhibited by β-lactams, which act on the cell wall rather than on DNA.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The 30S ribosomal subunit is bound by aminoglycosides and tetracyclines, which block protein synthesis.

questions.topicName: DNA gyrase and Folic acid inhibitors– 2 of 2: Fluoroquinolones

questions.stem: In the laboratory, a fluoroquinolone is added to purified bacterial DNA gyrase acting on plasmid DNA. The enzyme continues to cut the DNA backbone but the cut strands are no longer restored. Inhibition of which of the following enzyme domains best explains this observation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The ATPase domain that supplies energy for supercoiling

choices.label: B
choices.text: The helicase domain that separates parental strands

choices.label: C
choices.text: The ligase domain that reseals the nicked strand

choices.label: D
choices.text: The nuclease domain that nicks the DNA strand

choices.label: E
choices.text: The primase domain that lays down RNA primers

explanation.summary: Fluoroquinolones inhibit the ligase domain of type II topoisomerases while leaving the nuclease domain active.
explanation.whyCorrect: Both DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV carry two kinds of domains: a nuclease domain that nicks a DNA strand so the DNA can untwist, and a ligase domain that repairs that nick. Fluoroquinolones target and inhibit the ligase domain, so the nuclease keeps nicking DNA with the repair mechanism removed. The enzyme is effectively converted into a DNA shredder.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An ATPase block would stop the enzyme altogether rather than leave unrepaired cuts accumulating.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Helicase is a separate replication enzyme and is not a domain of the type II topoisomerases.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The nuclease domain remains active; if it were inhibited, no cuts would be made at all.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Primase synthesizes RNA primers and is not part of DNA gyrase or topoisomerase IV.

questions.topicName: DNA gyrase and Folic acid inhibitors– 2 of 2: Fluoroquinolones

questions.stem: A microbiologist exposes a culture of Escherichia coli to levofloxacin. The bacterial chromosome accumulates unrepaired breaks, replication stops, and the organisms are killed rather than merely prevented from dividing. Which of the following best explains this bactericidal effect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The drug binds the ribosome and causes misreading of messenger RNA

choices.label: B
choices.text: The drug blocks DNA repair while the enzyme keeps cutting the DNA

choices.label: C
choices.text: The drug blocks the cross-linking of peptidoglycan in the cell wall

choices.label: D
choices.text: The drug inserts into the membrane and causes leakage of cytoplasm

choices.label: E
choices.text: The drug prevents folate-dependent synthesis of thymidine for DNA

explanation.summary: Blocking the ligase domain turns type II topoisomerases into DNA shredders, halting replication and killing the cell.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because fluoroquinolones inhibit the repair (ligase) function while the nuclease continues to nick the DNA, the enzymes effectively shred the chromosome. DNA replication is halted and the bacterial cell dies, which explains the bactericidal nature of the class. This is distinct from bacteriostatic agents that merely stop growth.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ribosomal misreading of mRNA is the mechanism of aminoglycosides and does not involve DNA breaks.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Peptidoglycan cross-linking is inhibited by β-lactams, a different class with a different target.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Membrane disruption with leakage of cytoplasmic contents describes agents such as polymyxins.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Folate-dependent thymidine synthesis is blocked by the folic acid synthesis inhibitors, not by fluoroquinolones.

questions.topicName: DNA gyrase and Folic acid inhibitors– 2 of 2: Fluoroquinolones

questions.stem: Bacterial type II topoisomerases perform several overlapping functions on the chromosome. Which of the following activities is unique to DNA gyrase?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cutting one DNA strand using an intrinsic nuclease domain

choices.label: B
choices.text: Introducing negative supercoils into the bacterial chromosome

choices.label: C
choices.text: Relaxing negative supercoils that have formed in the DNA

choices.label: D
choices.text: Resealing a cut DNA strand using an intrinsic ligase domain

choices.label: E
choices.text: Separating two completed daughter chromosomes from each other

explanation.summary: Only DNA gyrase can create negative supercoils, which offset the positive supercoiling generated by replication.
explanation.whyCorrect: DNA gyrase uniquely creates negative supercoils, which help prepare the chromosome for the tension formed during DNA replication. When the strands of the helix are pulled apart, the DNA ahead winds tighter into positive supercoils, and gyrase counteracts this. Topoisomerase IV cannot introduce negative supercoils.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Both gyrase and topoisomerase IV possess a nuclease domain that nicks DNA.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Relaxation of negative supercoils is performed by topoisomerase IV and is shared by other topoisomerases.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Both gyrase and topoisomerase IV possess a ligase domain that repairs the nick.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Separating completed daughter chromosomes is decatenation, the role of topoisomerase IV.

questions.topicName: DNA gyrase and Folic acid inhibitors– 2 of 2: Fluoroquinolones

questions.stem: At the end of replication a circular bacterial chromosome remains physically interlinked with its newly synthesized copy, and the two rings must be separated before the cell can divide. Which of the following enzyme activities accomplishes this separation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: DNA gyrase introducing negative supercoils ahead of the fork

choices.label: B
choices.text: Helicase unwinding the parental duplex at the origin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ligase sealing the Okazaki fragments of the lagging strand

choices.label: D
choices.text: Primase synthesizing RNA primers on the leading strand

choices.label: E
choices.text: Topoisomerase IV passing one strand through the other

explanation.summary: Decatenation of the two completed bacterial chromosomes is the distinctive role of topoisomerase IV.
explanation.whyCorrect: Topoisomerase IV plays a role in decatenation, that is, separating two completed bacterial chromosomes by passing one strand through the other. This progressively reduces the interlinking braids until the two rings are free. Fluoroquinolones that preferentially inhibit topoisomerase IV therefore block the final step of chromosome segregation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Negative supercoiling by gyrase manages torsional tension but does not unlink completed chromosomes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Helicase separates the two parental strands at the start of replication, not the finished daughter rings.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ligase joins Okazaki fragments within a strand and cannot unlink two interlocked circles.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Primase lays down RNA primers to start synthesis and has no role in decatenation.

questions.topicName: DNA gyrase and Folic acid inhibitors– 2 of 2: Fluoroquinolones

questions.stem: Fluoroquinolones take their name from the addition of a fluorine atom to an older core compound. Which of the following is the original quinolone, now no longer on the market?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ciprofloxacin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Levofloxacin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Moxifloxacin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nalidixic acid

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ofloxacin

explanation.summary: Nalidixic acid is the original, non-fluorinated quinolone and is no longer marketed.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fluoroquinolones are a fluorinated form of quinolone, their core component. Nalidixic acid is presented as an original quinolone that is no longer on the market, in contrast to ciprofloxacin, which is commonly prescribed. The fluorinated derivatives largely replaced it.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ciprofloxacin is a fluorinated quinolone that remains one of the most commonly prescribed agents of the class.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Levofloxacin is a currently marketed fluoroquinolone and is the most commonly used respiratory agent.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Moxifloxacin is a currently marketed respiratory fluoroquinolone known for QTc prolongation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ofloxacin is a fluorinated quinolone still in use and is not the original core compound.

questions.topicName: DNA gyrase and Folic acid inhibitors– 2 of 2: Fluoroquinolones

questions.stem: A patient with a severe gram-negative infection is treated with a β-lactam in addition to a fluoroquinolone, and the combination clears the infection more efficiently than either agent alone. Which of the following best explains this synergy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The fluoroquinolone increases expression of the penicillin-binding proteins

choices.label: B
choices.text: The fluoroquinolone inhibits the β-lactamases that would destroy the β-lactam

choices.label: C
choices.text: The β-lactam blocks the efflux pumps that export the fluoroquinolone

choices.label: D
choices.text: The β-lactam disrupts the cell wall so the fluoroquinolone enters more easily

choices.label: E
choices.text: The β-lactam raises intracellular pH so the fluoroquinolone stays ionized

explanation.summary: β-Lactams inhibit cell wall synthesis, which makes it easier for fluoroquinolones to enter the bacterium and reach their target enzymes.
explanation.whyCorrect: The efficiency of fluoroquinolones can be increased by using synergistic medications together. β-Lactam antibiotics inhibit bacterial cell wall synthesis, allowing fluoroquinolones to have an easier time entering bacterial cells to reach their target enzymes. The two drugs therefore act at different steps that reinforce one another.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Increasing penicillin-binding protein expression would not enhance fluoroquinolone activity.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fluoroquinolones act on type II topoisomerases and have no activity against β-lactamases.
whyWrongByChoice.C: β-Lactams do not inhibit the efflux pumps that bacteria use to export fluoroquinolones.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Synergy is explained by easier entry through a damaged cell wall, not by an intracellular pH shift.

questions.topicName: DNA gyrase and Folic acid inhibitors– 2 of 2: Fluoroquinolones

questions.stem: A Pseudomonas aeruginosa isolate that was previously susceptible now grows in the presence of ciprofloxacin. Intracellular drug concentrations are far lower than in the susceptible parent strain, while the sequences of the gyrase and topoisomerase IV genes are unchanged. Which of the following best accounts for the resistance?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A point mutation in the gyrase subunit that binds the drug

choices.label: B
choices.text: Acetylation of the drug by a plasmid-encoded transferase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Active transport of the drug out of the cell by efflux pumps

choices.label: D
choices.text: Enzymatic cleavage of the drug by a bacterial hydrolase

choices.label: E
choices.text: Loss of the porin channels required for folate uptake

explanation.summary: One of the two main routes of fluoroquinolone resistance is efflux of the drug out of the bacterial cell by active transport.
explanation.whyCorrect: In general there are two main ways resistance develops to fluoroquinolones: active transport of the drug out of bacterial cells through efflux pumps, and alteration of the target binding site. A low intracellular concentration with a normal target sequence points to efflux. Pseudomonas aeruginosa is specifically noted as the most commonly resistant gram-negative organism.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A target mutation would leave intracellular drug levels normal, which is not what the assay shows.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Acetylating transferases inactivate aminoglycosides, not fluoroquinolones, and would not lower uptake.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hydrolytic destruction of the drug is not described as a mechanism of fluoroquinolone resistance.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Porin loss affecting folate uptake is unrelated to fluoroquinolones, which do not act on folate synthesis.

questions.topicName: DNA gyrase and Folic acid inhibitors– 2 of 2: Fluoroquinolones

questions.stem: Sequencing of a fluoroquinolone-resistant clinical isolate shows a chromosomal point mutation that changes an amino acid in a subunit of topoisomerase IV. Drug accumulation inside the bacterial cell is normal. Which of the following resistance mechanisms does this represent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alteration of the drug's target binding site

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased permeability of the outer membrane

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inactivation of the drug by a bacterial enzyme

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased export of the drug through efflux pumps

choices.label: E
choices.text: Overproduction of the drug's normal substrate

explanation.summary: Chromosomal mutation of a gyrase or topoisomerase IV subunit alters the target binding site and confers fluoroquinolone resistance.
explanation.whyCorrect: The second main route of resistance is alteration of the target binding site, specifically the topoisomerase IV or DNA gyrase subunits, by chromosomal mutation. The change can be chromosomal or integrated by way of plasmids acquired from nearby bacterial cells. Normal intracellular drug levels with an altered enzyme sequence identify this mechanism rather than efflux.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Reduced outer membrane permeability would also lower intracellular drug, not leave it normal.
whyWrongByChoice.C: No drug-inactivating enzyme is implied, and drug levels inside the cell are normal.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Efflux would reduce intracellular drug accumulation, which the assay shows is unchanged.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Fluoroquinolones act on an enzyme rather than competing with a substrate that could be overproduced.

questions.topicName: DNA gyrase and Folic acid inhibitors– 2 of 2: Fluoroquinolones

questions.stem: An intensive care unit reports that fluoroquinolone resistance appeared in several unrelated gram-negative species within a few weeks of one another. Which of the following best explains how resistance spread so rapidly across different organisms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Conversion of the antibiotic to an inactive metabolite by host enzymes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Independent spontaneous mutations arising in each separate species

choices.label: C
choices.text: Selection of pre-existing resistant clones by antibiotic pressure alone

choices.label: D
choices.text: Transfer of plasmids carrying resistance genes between bacteria

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vertical inheritance of resistance genes from parent to daughter cells

explanation.summary: Plasmids are little loops of genetic code acquired from nearby bacteria, and they let resistance spread quickly through a bacterial population.
explanation.whyCorrect: Target site alterations may be chromosomal or integrated by way of plasmids, small loops of genetic code acquired from nearby bacterial cells. Once one bacterium becomes resistant, the spread of resistance mechanisms via plasmids may quickly protect a large population. This horizontal transfer explains near-simultaneous resistance in unrelated species.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Host metabolism of the antibiotic is a pharmacokinetic issue and is not a bacterial resistance mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Simultaneous independent mutation in several unrelated species within weeks is far less likely than plasmid spread.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Selection pressure alone does not explain how the same resistance determinant appears across species.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vertical inheritance passes genes only within a lineage and cannot cross between different species.

questions.topicName: DNA gyrase and Folic acid inhibitors– 2 of 2: Fluoroquinolones

questions.stem: Fluoroquinolone resistance is widespread among gram-positive organisms. Which of the following is the most frequent gram-positive culprit?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Group A Streptococcus pyogenes from the pharynx

choices.label: B
choices.text: Listeria monocytogenes from food-borne exposure

choices.label: C
choices.text: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Penicillin-resistant Streptococcus pneumoniae

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium

explanation.summary: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus is the most frequent gram-positive organism with fluoroquinolone resistance.
explanation.whyCorrect: Resistance to fluoroquinolones is unfortunately widespread among both gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria. Among gram-positive organisms, methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus is the most frequent culprit. This is one reason fluoroquinolones are not relied on as monotherapy for suspected staphylococcal infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Streptococcus pyogenes is not cited as a common source of fluoroquinolone resistance.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Listeria monocytogenes is not named among the organisms driving fluoroquinolone resistance.
whyWrongByChoice.D: S. pneumoniae is the organism the respiratory fluoroquinolones are valued for covering, not the leading resistant gram-positive.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Enterococcus faecium is not identified as the most frequent gram-positive fluoroquinolone-resistant organism.

questions.topicName: DNA gyrase and Folic acid inhibitors– 2 of 2: Fluoroquinolones

questions.stem: A hospital antibiogram shows that among gram-negative isolates, one organism accounts for the largest share of ciprofloxacin resistance. Which of the following is most likely that organism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Escherichia coli

choices.label: B
choices.text: Haemophilus influenzae

choices.label: C
choices.text: Klebsiella pneumoniae

choices.label: D
choices.text: Proteus mirabilis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pseudomonas aeruginosa

explanation.summary: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is the most commonly fluoroquinolone-resistant gram-negative bacterium.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among gram-negative bacteria, Pseudomonas aeruginosa is the most commonly resistant organism to fluoroquinolones. This matters clinically because levofloxacin is chosen among the respiratory fluoroquinolones partly for its better Pseudomonas coverage. Susceptibility testing is therefore important before relying on a fluoroquinolone for pseudomonal infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Escherichia coli is a common urinary pathogen but is not named as the most commonly resistant gram-negative.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Haemophilus influenzae is not cited among the organisms driving fluoroquinolone resistance.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Klebsiella pneumoniae is not identified as the leading fluoroquinolone-resistant gram-negative organism.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Proteus mirabilis is not identified as the most commonly resistant gram-negative bacterium.

questions.topicName: DNA gyrase and Folic acid inhibitors– 2 of 2: Fluoroquinolones

questions.stem: Public health surveillance has documented more recent outbreaks of fluoroquinolone-resistant gram-negative organisms beyond the longstanding culprits. Which of the following pairs of organisms represents this newer pattern of resistance?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bacteroides fragilis and Prevotella melaninogenica

choices.label: B
choices.text: Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae

choices.label: C
choices.text: Haemophilus influenzae and Moraxella catarrhalis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Legionella pneumophila and Bordetella pertussis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Campylobacter jejuni

explanation.summary: Outbreaks of more resistant gram-negative organisms, specifically Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Campylobacter jejuni, have developed more recently.
explanation.whyCorrect: Beyond Pseudomonas aeruginosa, outbreaks of more resistant gram-negative organisms such as Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Campylobacter jejuni have developed more recently. Plasmid-mediated spread allows such resistance to protect a large population quickly once it appears. This has changed empiric therapy for gonorrhea and for invasive Campylobacter infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: These anaerobes are not cited among the organisms with newly developed fluoroquinolone resistance.
whyWrongByChoice.B: These are common gram-negative pathogens but are not the pair identified with newer fluoroquinolone resistance outbreaks.
whyWrongByChoice.C: These respiratory organisms are not named among the newly resistant gram-negative outbreaks.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Legionella and Bordetella are not identified as sources of emerging fluoroquinolone resistance.

questions.topicName: DNA gyrase and Folic acid inhibitors– 2 of 2: Fluoroquinolones

questions.stem: No formal grouping of the fluoroquinolones exists, but some agents are termed respiratory fluoroquinolones. Which of the following sets of drugs makes up this group?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, and ofloxacin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ciprofloxacin, norfloxacin, and ofloxacin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Levofloxacin, ciprofloxacin, and gatifloxacin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, and gatifloxacin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nalidixic acid, norfloxacin, and ofloxacin

explanation.summary: The respiratory fluoroquinolones are levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, and gatifloxacin.
explanation.whyCorrect: The group termed respiratory fluoroquinolones includes levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, and gatifloxacin, the last of which is available only in ophthalmic form in the United States. They are called respiratory fluoroquinolones because of their coverage against Streptococcus pneumoniae. Ciprofloxacin, norfloxacin, and ofloxacin form the other important group.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ciprofloxacin and ofloxacin are not respiratory fluoroquinolones, so this set is mixed.
whyWrongByChoice.B: These are the other important fluoroquinolones and are not the respiratory group.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ciprofloxacin is rarely used for respiratory infections and does not belong to this group.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nalidixic acid is the original quinolone and is no longer marketed; none of these is a respiratory agent.

questions.topicName: DNA gyrase and Folic acid inhibitors– 2 of 2: Fluoroquinolones

questions.stem: A group of fluoroquinolones is designated as respiratory agents on the basis of reliable activity against a single organism. Which of the following organisms gives them that name?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Clostridioides difficile

choices.label: B
choices.text: Escherichia coli

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pseudomonas aeruginosa

choices.label: D
choices.text: Staphylococcus aureus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Streptococcus pneumoniae

explanation.summary: Levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, and gatifloxacin are termed respiratory fluoroquinolones because of their coverage against Streptococcus pneumoniae.
explanation.whyCorrect: Levofloxacin and moxifloxacin are key antibiotics for respiratory infections, and they are termed respiratory fluoroquinolones because of their coverage against S. pneumoniae. This distinguishes them from ciprofloxacin, which is rarely used for respiratory infections. Their use above the diaphragm separates them from other systemic fluoroquinolones.

whyWrongByChoice.A: C. difficile is a consequence of fluoroquinolone-induced dysbiosis, not an organism these drugs are chosen to cover.
whyWrongByChoice.B: E. coli is a urinary and systemic pathogen and is not the organism behind the respiratory designation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pseudomonas coverage explains why levofloxacin is preferred within the group, not why the group is called respiratory.
whyWrongByChoice.D: S. aureus is the most frequent gram-positive organism showing fluoroquinolone resistance, not the basis for the name.

questions.topicName: DNA gyrase and Folic acid inhibitors– 2 of 2: Fluoroquinolones

questions.stem: Levofloxacin is the most commonly used of the respiratory fluoroquinolones. Which of the following best explains this preference over moxifloxacin and gatifloxacin?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A long half-life that permits once-weekly oral dosing

choices.label: B
choices.text: Absence of any interaction with cation-containing antacids

choices.label: C
choices.text: Better Pseudomonas coverage and a lesser side-effect profile

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lack of cartilage toxicity permitting routine pediatric use

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reliable activity against Clostridioides difficile colitis

explanation.summary: Levofloxacin is favored among the respiratory fluoroquinolones for better Pseudomonas coverage and a milder side-effect profile.
explanation.whyCorrect: Levofloxacin is the most common of the respiratory fluoroquinolones because it has better Pseudomonas coverage and a lesser side-effect profile than moxifloxacin and gatifloxacin. Moxifloxacin in particular carries the greatest risk of QTc prolongation within the class. Gatifloxacin is only available in ophthalmic form in the United States.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fluoroquinolones are not dosed once weekly, and dosing interval is not the basis for this preference.
whyWrongByChoice.B: All fluoroquinolones are chelated by divalent and trivalent cations found in antacids and supplements.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cartilage erosion and arthropathy are class effects, which is why fluoroquinolones are generally avoided in children.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Fluoroquinolones promote C. difficile overgrowth through dysbiosis rather than treating it.

questions.topicName: DNA gyrase and Folic acid inhibitors– 2 of 2: Fluoroquinolones

questions.stem: A pharmacist explains that one of the respiratory fluoroquinolones cannot be dispensed as a systemic agent in the United States and is marketed there only as an eye preparation. Which of the following is that drug?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ciprofloxacin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gatifloxacin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Levofloxacin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Moxifloxacin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ofloxacin

explanation.summary: Gatifloxacin is a respiratory fluoroquinolone available only in ophthalmic form in the United States.
explanation.whyCorrect: The respiratory fluoroquinolones include levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, and gatifloxacin, the last of which is only available in ophthalmic form in the United States. Levofloxacin and moxifloxacin remain the systemic respiratory agents. Fluoroquinolones can be dosed orally, parenterally, or topically as cream or ophthalmic preparations.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ciprofloxacin is widely available systemically and is the most common of the non-respiratory fluoroquinolones.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Levofloxacin is available systemically and is the most commonly used respiratory fluoroquinolone.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Moxifloxacin is available as a systemic respiratory fluoroquinolone.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ofloxacin is one of the other important fluoroquinolones and is not restricted to eye preparations.

questions.topicName: DNA gyrase and Folic acid inhibitors– 2 of 2: Fluoroquinolones

questions.stem: Which of the following fluoroquinolones has been withdrawn from the United States market although it continues to be used elsewhere in the world?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ciprofloxacin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Levofloxacin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Moxifloxacin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Norfloxacin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ofloxacin

explanation.summary: Norfloxacin has been withdrawn from the US market but is still used in other countries.
explanation.whyCorrect: The other important fluoroquinolones besides the respiratory agents are ciprofloxacin, norfloxacin, and ofloxacin. Notably, norfloxacin has been withdrawn from the US market but is used elsewhere. Ciprofloxacin is the most effective of this group when given systemically and is therefore the most commonly used.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ciprofloxacin is the most commonly used agent of its group and remains on the market.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Levofloxacin is widely used and is the most common respiratory fluoroquinolone.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Moxifloxacin remains available as a respiratory fluoroquinolone despite its QTc risk.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ofloxacin remains one of the important fluoroquinolones in use and was not withdrawn.

questions.topicName: DNA gyrase and Folic acid inhibitors– 2 of 2: Fluoroquinolones

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with a known 4.8-cm infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm needs oral therapy for a urinary tract infection. Which of the following adverse outcomes makes a fluoroquinolone a poor choice in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Accelerated formation of calcium oxalate kidney stones

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hemolysis in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hypertensive crisis from excessive catecholamine release

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased risk of aortic aneurysm enlargement and dissection

choices.label: E
choices.text: Irreversible pulmonary fibrosis with prolonged exposure

explanation.summary: Fluoroquinolones increase the risk of aortic aneurysm and dissection and are best avoided in patients at risk.
explanation.whyCorrect: Use of fluoroquinolones has been shown to increase the risk of aortic aneurysms or dissection. In patients with risk of aortic aneurysms it is best to avoid fluoroquinolones. A patient with a known abdominal aortic aneurysm falls squarely into that group, and an alternative agent should be selected.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Kidney stone formation is not among the adverse effects attributed to fluoroquinolones.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemolysis in G6PD deficiency is not listed among fluoroquinolone adverse reactions.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fluoroquinolones are not associated with catecholamine release or hypertensive crisis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pulmonary fibrosis is not a recognized fluoroquinolone adverse effect.

questions.topicName: DNA gyrase and Folic acid inhibitors– 2 of 2: Fluoroquinolones

questions.stem: Clinicians often divide the systemic fluoroquinolones according to the body region in which they are typically used. Which of the following best describes that division?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All fluoroquinolones are interchangeable for infection at any body site

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ciprofloxacin and levofloxacin are both reserved for sites above the diaphragm

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ciprofloxacin is used above the diaphragm and levofloxacin below it

choices.label: D
choices.text: Levofloxacin and moxifloxacin are used above the diaphragm, ciprofloxacin below

choices.label: E
choices.text: Moxifloxacin is used for urinary infections and ciprofloxacin for pneumonia

explanation.summary: Levofloxacin and moxifloxacin are used for respiratory infections above the diaphragm; ciprofloxacin is used for systemic infections below it.
explanation.whyCorrect: While ciprofloxacin is rarely used for respiratory infections, levofloxacin and moxifloxacin are key antibiotics for them. Their use in respiratory infections, above the diaphragm, separates them from other systemic fluoroquinolones such as ciprofloxacin, which is used for other systemic infections below the diaphragm. Ciprofloxacin is the most effective of its group when given systemically.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The agents differ meaningfully in spectrum and site of use and are not interchangeable.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ciprofloxacin is used for systemic infections below the diaphragm, not above it.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This reverses the rule; ciprofloxacin is rarely used for infections above the diaphragm.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This reverses the usual roles of moxifloxacin and ciprofloxacin.

questions.topicName: DNA gyrase and Folic acid inhibitors– 2 of 2: Fluoroquinolones

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman treated with oral ciprofloxacin for a urinary tract infection fails to improve, and serum drug concentrations are unexpectedly low. She reports taking an aluminum- and magnesium-containing antacid with each dose. Which of the following best explains the treatment failure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The antacid displaces the antibiotic from plasma protein binding sites

choices.label: B
choices.text: The antacid induces hepatic enzymes that clear the antibiotic

choices.label: C
choices.text: The antacid raises gastric pH and chemically degrades the antibiotic

choices.label: D
choices.text: The antacid stimulates renal tubular secretion of the antibiotic

choices.label: E
choices.text: The antacid's cations chelate the antibiotic and block absorption

explanation.summary: Divalent and trivalent cations in antacids chelate fluoroquinolones and decrease their absorption.
explanation.whyCorrect: While food overall has little effect on fluoroquinolone absorption, divalent or trivalent cations such as aluminum, magnesium, and calcium found in antacids can chelate with fluoroquinolones and decrease absorption. Iron and mineral supplements and multivitamins do the same. The result is subtherapeutic drug levels and treatment failure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Protein-binding displacement would raise free drug rather than lower measured concentrations.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Antacids do not induce hepatic enzymes; the interaction occurs in the gut lumen before absorption.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The problem is chelation of the drug by cations, not degradation caused by a change in gastric pH.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Antacids do not increase renal tubular secretion of fluoroquinolones.

questions.topicName: DNA gyrase and Folic acid inhibitors– 2 of 2: Fluoroquinolones

questions.stem: A patient who takes a daily multivitamin with iron is prescribed oral levofloxacin. Which of the following instructions is most appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Double the antibiotic dose to overcome reduced absorption

choices.label: B
choices.text: Stop the multivitamin permanently while taking the antibiotic

choices.label: C
choices.text: Take both medications together with a full glass of milk

choices.label: D
choices.text: Take the antibiotic 4 to 6 hours after the multivitamin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Take the antibiotic on an empty stomach and avoid all food

explanation.summary: Fluoroquinolones should be separated from cation-containing products by 4 to 6 hours.
explanation.whyCorrect: Iron and mineral supplements and multivitamins decrease fluoroquinolone absorption through chelation. To avoid these interactions, fluoroquinolones are given 4 to 6 hours after these medications. Separating the doses preserves absorption without requiring the supplement to be stopped.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dose doubling is not the recommended way to manage a chelation interaction.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Permanent discontinuation is unnecessary because separating the doses in time solves the problem.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Taking them together maximizes chelation, and milk adds calcium, which worsens the interaction.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Food overall has little effect on fluoroquinolone absorption, so avoiding all food is not the issue.

questions.topicName: DNA gyrase and Folic acid inhibitors– 2 of 2: Fluoroquinolones

questions.stem: In a pharmacokinetic study, a fluoroquinolone is measured in lung and prostate tissue and is found at concentrations exceeding the simultaneous peak serum level. Which of the following properties of the class best explains this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A very high volume of distribution into body tissues

choices.label: B
choices.text: Active secretion into the renal proximal tubule

choices.label: C
choices.text: Enterohepatic recirculation through the biliary tract

choices.label: D
choices.text: Extensive binding to circulating plasma albumin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Negligible oral bioavailability requiring intravenous dosing

explanation.summary: Fluoroquinolones have a very high volume of distribution, so tissue concentrations can exceed peak serum levels.
explanation.whyCorrect: When taken orally, fluoroquinolones are quickly absorbed through the gut wall, pass the hepatic circulation, and enter the blood to reach the systemic circulation. As a class they have a very high volume of distribution, and concentrations in some tissues surpass the peak serum concentration. This is why they penetrate difficult sites, including the central nervous system, so well.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Renal tubular secretion is a route of elimination and would not raise lung or prostate concentrations.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Enterohepatic recirculation prolongs exposure but does not explain tissue levels above peak serum levels.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Heavy plasma protein binding would keep drug in the vascular compartment rather than drive it into tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Fluoroquinolones are well absorbed orally, which is why oral therapy is standard for many infections.

questions.topicName: DNA gyrase and Folic acid inhibitors– 2 of 2: Fluoroquinolones

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease maintained on theophylline is started on ciprofloxacin for a urinary infection. Two days later he has nausea, tremor, and palpitations. Which of the following best explains his symptoms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ciprofloxacin displaced theophylline from albumin binding sites

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ciprofloxacin increased the renal clearance of theophylline

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ciprofloxacin inhibited cytochrome P450 1A2, raising theophylline

choices.label: D
choices.text: Theophylline blocked the gut absorption of ciprofloxacin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Theophylline induced hepatic conversion of ciprofloxacin to a toxin

explanation.summary: Ciprofloxacin inhibits cytochrome P450 isozyme 1A2, which is used to eliminate theophylline, so theophylline accumulates.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fluoroquinolones, particularly ciprofloxacin, inhibit cytochrome P450 isozyme 1A2, which is also used in the elimination of theophylline and caffeine. Because fluoroquinolones inhibit this enzyme, dosing of medications metabolized by it should be adjusted, and theophylline in particular should have its dose significantly decreased when ciprofloxacin is started. Nausea, tremor, and palpitations are classic features of theophylline excess.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The interaction is metabolic inhibition at CYP1A2 rather than displacement from albumin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ciprofloxacin impairs theophylline elimination; it does not accelerate clearance.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reduced ciprofloxacin absorption would cause antibiotic failure, not symptoms of theophylline toxicity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Theophylline is not described as inducing metabolism of ciprofloxacin to a toxic product.

questions.topicName: DNA gyrase and Folic acid inhibitors– 2 of 2: Fluoroquinolones

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman completes a course of ciprofloxacin and now reports vulvar itching with a thick white vaginal discharge. Which of the following best explains this complication?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A type I hypersensitivity reaction to the fluoroquinolone

choices.label: B
choices.text: Direct irritant toxicity of the drug on the vaginal epithelium

choices.label: C
choices.text: Disturbance of normal vaginal flora allowing candidal overgrowth

choices.label: D
choices.text: Drug-induced estrogen deficiency thinning the vaginal mucosa

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reactivation of a latent sexually transmitted bacterial infection

explanation.summary: Fluoroquinolones disturb normal vaginal flora, which increases the risk of candida vaginitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The most common fluoroquinolone side effects involve divergence from bacterial homeostasis, and disturbance of normal vaginal flora may lead to an increased risk of candida vaginitis. The same loss of normal flora in the gut allows Clostridioides difficile to proliferate. If a patient experiences an adverse reaction, the fluoroquinolone should be discontinued.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Type I hypersensitivity presents with urticaria, angioedema, or anaphylaxis, not candidal discharge.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Systemically administered ciprofloxacin does not cause direct irritant injury to vaginal epithelium.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fluoroquinolones do not lower estrogen levels or cause atrophic vaginal changes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Antibiotic therapy does not reactivate a latent bacterial sexually transmitted infection in this way.

questions.topicName: DNA gyrase and Folic acid inhibitors– 2 of 2: Fluoroquinolones

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most common adverse effect of fluoroquinolone therapy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Peripheral neuropathy of the hands and feet

choices.label: B
choices.text: Prolongation of the QTc interval

choices.label: C
choices.text: Stevens-Johnson syndrome with mucosal sloughing

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tendon rupture at the Achilles insertion

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transient, mild gastrointestinal upset

explanation.summary: The most common adverse effect of fluoroquinolone use is transient or mild gastrointestinal upset.
explanation.whyCorrect: The most common adverse effect with fluoroquinolone use is transient or mild GI upset. Disturbances in the gut microbiome, or gut dysbiosis, lead to the classic gastrointestinal side effects of nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. The more dramatic toxicities of the class are far less frequent.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Peripheral neuropathy is specifically described as a rare adverse drug reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.B: QTc prolongation is a recognized risk, chiefly with moxifloxacin, but it is not the most common effect.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis are rare hypersensitivity reactions.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tendinopathy and tendon rupture are uncommon, though real, considerations in patients treated with fluoroquinolones.

questions.topicName: DNA gyrase and Folic acid inhibitors– 2 of 2: Fluoroquinolones

questions.stem: A 74-year-old man develops profuse watery diarrhea, crampy abdominal pain, and leukocytosis 6 days after starting levofloxacin for pneumonia. Which of the following organisms is the most likely cause of his diarrhea?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Campylobacter jejuni

choices.label: B
choices.text: Clostridioides difficile

choices.label: C
choices.text: Escherichia coli O157:H7

choices.label: D
choices.text: Norovirus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Salmonella enteritidis

explanation.summary: Fluoroquinolone-induced loss of normal gut flora allows Clostridioides difficile to proliferate and cause colitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Disturbances in the gut microbiome, or gut dysbiosis, produce the classic gastrointestinal side effects of fluoroquinolones. A lack of competition by normal gut flora may allow Clostridioides difficile to proliferate, leading to overgrowth and C difficile colitis. New profuse diarrhea with leukocytosis during antibiotic therapy should prompt this consideration.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Campylobacter jejuni is a food-borne pathogen and is noted for developing fluoroquinolone resistance, not for antibiotic-associated colitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: E. coli O157:H7 causes bloody diarrhea from contaminated food, not an antibiotic-related overgrowth syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Norovirus causes brief outbreaks of vomiting and diarrhea unrelated to antibiotic exposure.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Salmonella enteritidis causes food-borne gastroenteritis rather than antibiotic-associated colitis.

questions.topicName: DNA gyrase and Folic acid inhibitors– 2 of 2: Fluoroquinolones

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman being treated with moxifloxacin collapses. Telemetry shows a polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with a twisting QRS axis, and her preceding tracing showed a prolonged QTc. Which of the following drug effects is most likely responsible?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blockade of cardiac sodium channels slowing conduction velocity

choices.label: B
choices.text: Blockade of L-type calcium channels depressing contractility

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inhibition of cardiac potassium channels prolonging repolarization

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inhibition of the sodium-potassium ATPase raising intracellular calcium

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stimulation of β1-adrenergic receptors increasing automaticity

explanation.summary: Moxifloxacin prolongs the QTc by inhibiting specific potassium channels, predisposing to torsades de pointes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Moxifloxacin, and other fluoroquinolones to a lesser degree, carry a risk of QTc prolongation leading to possible arrhythmias, most notably torsades de pointes. This occurs due to inhibition of specific potassium channels, which delays repolarization. A polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with a twisting axis in a patient with a long QTc is torsades.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Sodium channel blockade widens the QRS and slows conduction rather than prolonging repolarization.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Calcium channel blockade reduces contractility and rate and does not prolong the QT interval.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Na+/K+-ATPase inhibition is the mechanism of digoxin toxicity, not of fluoroquinolone-induced QTc prolongation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: β1 stimulation increases heart rate and contractility but is not the mechanism of fluoroquinolone-associated torsades.

questions.topicName: DNA gyrase and Folic acid inhibitors– 2 of 2: Fluoroquinolones

questions.stem: A patient is to receive a fluoroquinolone that is known to carry a risk of QT prolongation. Which of the following monitoring measures is recommended during therapy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Daily peak and trough drug levels

choices.label: B
choices.text: Electrocardiographic monitoring

choices.label: C
choices.text: Periodic audiometry testing

choices.label: D
choices.text: Serial serum creatinine measurement

choices.label: E
choices.text: Weekly liver function testing

explanation.summary: EKG monitoring is recommended for drugs that carry a risk of QT prolongation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because moxifloxacin and other fluoroquinolones can prolong the QTc and precipitate torsades de pointes, EKG monitoring is recommended for drugs that carry the risk of QT prolongation. Monitoring allows the interval to be followed and the drug stopped before an arrhythmia occurs. The mechanism is inhibition of specific cardiac potassium channels.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Peak and trough levels are used for narrow-therapeutic-index drugs such as aminoglycosides, not for this risk.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Audiometry monitors ototoxic drugs such as aminoglycosides, which is not a fluoroquinolone concern.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Serial creatinine measurement does not detect the cardiac conduction effect that is being monitored.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Routine liver function testing is not the monitoring recommended for QT-prolonging fluoroquinolones.

questions.topicName: DNA gyrase and Folic acid inhibitors– 2 of 2: Fluoroquinolones

questions.stem: An 80-year-old man becomes agitated and confused and cannot recall recent events several hours after receiving a single dose of ciprofloxacin. His metabolic panel and head CT are unremarkable. Which of the following properties of fluoroquinolones best explains this reaction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Accumulation of the drug from impaired biliary excretion

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chelation of magnesium within central nervous system synapses

choices.label: C
choices.text: Displacement of bilirubin from albumin in the aging brain

choices.label: D
choices.text: First-pass metabolism generating a neurotoxic metabolite

choices.label: E
choices.text: Very good penetration of the drug into the central nervous system

explanation.summary: Good CNS penetration by fluoroquinolones underlies neurologic side effects, which can follow even a single dose.
explanation.whyCorrect: Given their generally very good CNS penetration, side effects such as headache, dizziness, delirium, agitation, and memory impairment have been reported with just a single use of a fluoroquinolone. The elderly are particularly vulnerable to altered mental status. Seizures and peripheral neuropathy are rarer neurologic adverse reactions.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Impaired biliary excretion is not the described basis for fluoroquinolone neurotoxicity.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fluoroquinolones are chelated by cations in the gut lumen; they do not strip magnesium from CNS synapses.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Bilirubin displacement from albumin relates to kernicterus in neonates, not to delirium in the elderly.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The neurologic effects are attributed to drug penetration into the CNS rather than to a neurotoxic metabolite.

questions.topicName: DNA gyrase and Folic acid inhibitors– 2 of 2: Fluoroquinolones

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman treated with a fluoroquinolone 8 months ago still has burning numbness in both feet. Nerve conduction studies confirm a peripheral neuropathy. Which of the following best characterizes this adverse effect of fluoroquinolones?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is a common effect that resolves within days of stopping the drug

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a rare effect that may last years or even be permanent

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is an expected effect that does not warrant stopping the drug

choices.label: D
choices.text: It occurs only after months of continuous high-dose therapy

choices.label: E
choices.text: It reflects cartilage injury at the weight-bearing joints of the foot

explanation.summary: Fluoroquinolone-associated peripheral neuropathy is rare but can last from months to years or be permanent.
explanation.whyCorrect: Seizures and peripheral neuropathy are rare adverse drug reactions of fluoroquinolones. The peripheral neuropathy can last from months to years or be permanent. If a patient experiences an adverse reaction such as this, the fluoroquinolone should be discontinued.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The neuropathy is a rare reaction and characteristically persists long after the drug is stopped.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Any adverse reaction of this kind is an indication to discontinue the fluoroquinolone.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neurologic effects of fluoroquinolones have been reported after even a single use.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cartilage erosion and arthropathy are a separate musculoskeletal effect seen mainly in children.

questions.topicName: DNA gyrase and Folic acid inhibitors– 2 of 2: Fluoroquinolones

questions.stem: A 30-year-old landscaper is starting a 10-day course of a fluoroquinolone and asks what precautions he should take while working outdoors. Which of the following adverse effects should be discussed with him?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blue-green discoloration of the urine

choices.label: B
choices.text: Heat intolerance from impaired sweating

choices.label: C
choices.text: Night blindness from progressive retinal toxicity

choices.label: D
choices.text: Permanent gray discoloration of the teeth

choices.label: E
choices.text: Photosensitivity and phototoxic skin reactions

explanation.summary: Photosensitivity and phototoxicity are real concerns with fluoroquinolones, and sunscreen use is recommended.
explanation.whyCorrect: Photosensitivity and phototoxicity are real concerns for some patients taking fluoroquinolones, with sunscreen use being a definite recommendation, though its efficacy is questionable. Allergies and rashes affect roughly 1% to 2% of patients and worsen with prolonged treatment. A patient with heavy sun exposure should be counseled before starting therapy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fluoroquinolones are not associated with discoloration of the urine.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Impaired sweating and heat intolerance are anticholinergic effects, not fluoroquinolone effects.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Retinal toxicity and night blindness are not described among fluoroquinolone adverse effects.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tooth discoloration is associated with tetracyclines, not with fluoroquinolones.

questions.topicName: DNA gyrase and Folic acid inhibitors– 2 of 2: Fluoroquinolones

questions.stem: A child treated with a fluoroquinolone develops fever, painful erosions of the oral and conjunctival mucosa, and sloughing of large sheets of epidermis. He recovers after prolonged supportive care. Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term recommendation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Avoid fluoroquinolones for the rest of his life

choices.label: B
choices.text: Restrict fluoroquinolones only until he reaches adulthood

choices.label: C
choices.text: Resume the same fluoroquinolone at a reduced dose

choices.label: D
choices.text: Take an antihistamine before any future fluoroquinolone dose

choices.label: E
choices.text: Use a different fluoroquinolone with premedication

explanation.summary: After a severe hypersensitivity reaction such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis, fluoroquinolones must be avoided for life.
explanation.whyCorrect: More severe hypersensitivity reactions to fluoroquinolones, such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, are rare but have been reported. Patients affected should avoid taking fluoroquinolones for life. Rechallenge risks a recurrence that can be fatal.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The avoidance is lifelong and is not limited to childhood.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dose reduction does not prevent recurrence of a severe hypersensitivity reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Antihistamine pretreatment does not prevent Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Switching within the same class still risks recurrence, and premedication is not protective for these reactions.

questions.topicName: DNA gyrase and Folic acid inhibitors– 2 of 2: Fluoroquinolones

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy with cystic fibrosis has a Pseudomonas aeruginosa pulmonary exacerbation, and ciprofloxacin is prescribed despite the usual reluctance to give fluoroquinolones to children. Which of the following toxicities underlies that reluctance?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cartilage erosion and arthropathy of weight-bearing joints

choices.label: B
choices.text: Irreversible sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Kernicterus from displacement of bound bilirubin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Permanent staining of the developing permanent teeth

choices.label: E
choices.text: Suppression of linear growth at the epiphyseal plates

explanation.summary: Fluoroquinolones cause cartilage erosion and arthropathy in the weight-bearing joints of children, so they are generally avoided in this age group.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fluoroquinolones famously affect bones and tendons, especially in children, and cartilage erosion and arthropathy have been noted in children in weight-bearing joints. Because fluoroquinolones are rarely used in children, pediatric data are limited, but ciprofloxacin use in cystic fibrosis, where death from Pseudomonas infection is a weightier risk than long-term fluoroquinolone exposure, has supplied retrospective data. Risks and benefits should still be weighed for each patient.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Sensorineural hearing loss is a toxicity of aminoglycosides, not of fluoroquinolones.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Kernicterus from bilirubin displacement is a concern with sulfonamides in neonates.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tooth staining in children is characteristic of tetracyclines.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Epiphyseal growth suppression is not the described pediatric fluoroquinolone toxicity.

questions.topicName: DNA gyrase and Folic acid inhibitors– 2 of 2: Fluoroquinolones

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man starting levofloxacin is counseled about the risk of tendon injury. Which of the following tendons is most commonly involved in fluoroquinolone-associated tendinopathy and rupture?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Achilles tendon

choices.label: B
choices.text: Biceps tendon

choices.label: C
choices.text: Patellar tendon

choices.label: D
choices.text: Quadriceps tendon

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rotator cuff tendon

explanation.summary: Most cases of fluoroquinolone-associated tendinopathy and rupture involve the Achilles tendon.
explanation.whyCorrect: Tendinopathy and tendon rupture are uncommon but real considerations in those being treated with fluoroquinolones. Most cases involve the Achilles tendon, although other tendons may be affected. Patients should be warned to stop the drug and seek care if tendon pain develops.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Biceps tendon involvement is possible but is far less typical than Achilles involvement.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The patellar tendon may rarely be involved but is not the characteristic site.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The quadriceps tendon is not the tendon most commonly affected by fluoroquinolones.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Rotator cuff tendons are among the other tendons that may be affected, but not the most common.

questions.topicName: DNA gyrase and Folic acid inhibitors– 2 of 2: Fluoroquinolones

questions.stem: A 78-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes treated with glipizide is started on levofloxacin. Two days later she is found diaphoretic and confused; fingerstick glucose is 42 mg/dL. Which of the following fluoroquinolone adverse effects does this represent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Central nervous system toxicity from good CNS penetration

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dysglycemia, a known risk in elderly diabetic patients

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gut dysbiosis reducing absorption of dietary carbohydrate

choices.label: D
choices.text: Peripheral neuropathy involving the autonomic nerve fibers

choices.label: E
choices.text: QTc prolongation producing transient cerebral hypoperfusion

explanation.summary: Fluoroquinolones cause dysglycemia and carry a warning about hypoglycemia, particularly in elderly patients with diabetes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fluoroquinolones have been associated with both hyperglycemia and hypoglycemia. They now carry a warning about the risk of hypoglycemia, particularly in elderly patients with diabetes. A documented glucose of 42 mg/dL in such a patient shortly after starting levofloxacin fits this recognized adverse effect.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CNS penetration explains delirium and memory impairment but would not produce a glucose of 42 mg/dL.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gut dysbiosis causes nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea rather than clinically significant hypoglycemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fluoroquinolone peripheral neuropathy presents with sensory symptoms in the limbs, not with documented hypoglycemia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: QTc prolongation causes arrhythmia and syncope, and would not explain the measured low glucose.

questions.topicName: DNA gyrase and Folic acid inhibitors– 2 of 2: Fluoroquinolones

questions.stem: A 41-year-old woman has an 11-day history of facial pressure, purulent nasal discharge, and fever. Examination shows maxillary sinus tenderness, and acute bacterial sinusitis is diagnosed. Which of the following groups of organisms is most likely responsible for her infection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Proteus mirabilis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Listeria monocytogenes, Enterococcus faecalis, and Clostridioides difficile

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia trachomatis, and Rickettsia rickettsii

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Acinetobacter baumannii, and Serratia marcescens

choices.label: E
choices.text: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and Moraxella catarrhalis

explanation.summary: Acute bacterial sinusitis is usually caused by S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, and M. catarrhalis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acute bacterial sinusitis is an upper respiratory tract infection, and the three organisms that classically cause it are Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and Moraxella catarrhalis. This trio drives the choice of therapy, which must cover a gram-positive coccus plus two gram-negative respiratory organisms. Amoxicillin/clavulanate is therefore a very common treatment.

whyWrongByChoice.A: These Enterobacteriaceae cause urinary and intra-abdominal infections, not the typical upper respiratory tract picture of sinusitis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Listeria, Enterococcus, and C. difficile cause meningitis, urinary tract infection, and colitis respectively, not sinusitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: These atypical and rickettsial organisms cause atypical pneumonia, genital infection, and tick-borne illness rather than bacterial sinusitis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: These are hospital-associated gram-negative organisms seen in ventilated or severely ill patients, not causes of community sinusitis.

questions.topicName: Spectrum of Activity and Indications – 2: β-lactams and 30S Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man is diagnosed with acute bacterial sinusitis and needs an oral antibiotic that will cover Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and Moraxella catarrhalis. Which of the following is the most appropriate therapy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Amoxicillin-clavulanate

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gentamicin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Imipenem/cilastatin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Linezolid

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nafcillin

explanation.summary: Amoxicillin/clavulanate is the common treatment for acute bacterial sinusitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Aminopenicillins such as amoxicillin, when combined with a β-lactamase inhibitor like clavulanate, provide good gram-positive coverage plus good gram-negative coverage. That combination spans S. pneumoniae as well as H. influenzae and M. catarrhalis, which are the organisms of acute bacterial sinusitis. It is therefore a very common outpatient choice for this infection.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Gentamicin is an aminoglycoside with limited gram-positive activity and is not an oral agent for sinusitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Carbapenems are reserved for complicated infections such as hospital-acquired pneumonia and are not oral agents.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Linezolid covers gram-positive organisms only and provides no coverage of the gram-negative respiratory pathogens.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nafcillin is an antistaphylococcal penicillin that is not effective against many gram-negative bacteria such as H. influenzae.

questions.topicName: Spectrum of Activity and Indications – 2: β-lactams and 30S Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 19-year-old college student is admitted with fever, headache, and nuchal rigidity. Cerebrospinal fluid Gram stain shows gram-negative diplococci, and cultures grow Neisseria meningitidis. Which of the following antibiotics has activity against this organism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ampicillin-sulbactam

choices.label: B
choices.text: Linezolid

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nafcillin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oral vancomycin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Oxacillin

explanation.summary: Ampicillin combined with sulbactam is effective against Neisseria meningitidis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Aminopenicillins paired with a β-lactamase inhibitor extend their reach into gram-negative organisms. Ampicillin with sulbactam is specifically effective against Neisseria meningitidis, which causes bacterial meningitis and septicemia. The other listed agents act only on gram-positive bacteria.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Linezolid is a gram-positive agent and would not treat a gram-negative diplococcus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nafcillin is an antistaphylococcal penicillin and is not effective against many gram-negative bacteria, including Neisseria.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Oral vancomycin is not absorbed, acts only in the gut, and has no gram-negative activity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Oxacillin, like nafcillin, is aimed at staphylococci and lacks gram-negative coverage.

questions.topicName: Spectrum of Activity and Indications – 2: β-lactams and 30S Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man has a urinary tract infection, and ampicillin is started. Aminopenicillins retain useful gram-positive activity with one important exception. Which of the following organisms is reliably covered by ampicillin?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acinetobacter baumannii

choices.label: B
choices.text: Enterococcus faecalis

choices.label: C
choices.text: ESBL-producing Klebsiella pneumoniae

choices.label: D
choices.text: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pseudomonas aeruginosa

explanation.summary: Aminopenicillins cover gram-positive organisms including Enterococcus, but not MRSA.
explanation.whyCorrect: Amoxicillin and ampicillin provide good gram-positive coverage, and Enterococcus is specifically included in that spectrum. The single gram-positive exception is MRSA, which aminopenicillins do not cover. Enterococcal urinary tract infection is therefore a classic ampicillin indication.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acinetobacter is a resistant gram-negative organism outside the aminopenicillin spectrum.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Extended-spectrum β-lactamase producing Enterobacteriaceae are explicitly not covered by aminopenicillins.
whyWrongByChoice.D: MRSA is the named gram-positive exception to aminopenicillin coverage.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Aminopenicillins, even with a β-lactamase inhibitor, do not cover Pseudomonas.

questions.topicName: Spectrum of Activity and Indications – 2: β-lactams and 30S Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 70-year-old hospitalized woman with a catheter-associated urinary tract infection is treated with ampicillin-sulbactam but remains febrile. Urine culture grows an extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL)-producing Escherichia coli. Which of the following best explains the treatment failure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aminopenicillins act only on organisms growing anaerobically

choices.label: B
choices.text: Aminopenicillins are excreted unchanged and never reach the urine

choices.label: C
choices.text: Aminopenicillins cover only atypical intracellular pathogens

choices.label: D
choices.text: Aminopenicillins do not cover ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae

choices.label: E
choices.text: Aminopenicillins inhibit the 30S ribosome rather than the cell wall

explanation.summary: Aminopenicillins fail against ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae and against Pseudomonas.
explanation.whyCorrect: Amoxicillin and ampicillin, even with a β-lactamase inhibitor, do not cover extended-spectrum β-lactamase producing Enterobacteriaceae or Pseudomonas. ESBL organisms make β-lactamase enzymes that degrade these β-lactam antibiotics. Carbapenems are the reliable option once an ESBL producer is identified.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aminopenicillins are not restricted to anaerobic growth conditions; E. coli grows aerobically and is ordinarily within their spectrum.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Drug delivery to the urine is not the problem here; enzymatic degradation of the antibiotic is.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Aminopenicillins with an inhibitor cover many atypicals but are not limited to them; they are primarily cell-wall active agents.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Aminopenicillins are β-lactams that block cell wall synthesis; 30S inhibition describes aminoglycosides and tetracyclines.

questions.topicName: Spectrum of Activity and Indications – 2: β-lactams and 30S Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man in the intensive care unit develops fever and hypotension three days after abdominal surgery. Broad empiric coverage of gram-positive organisms, Enterobacteriaceae, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa is needed while cultures are pending. Which of the following single agents is most appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ampicillin-sulbactam

choices.label: B
choices.text: Aztreonam

choices.label: C
choices.text: Doxycycline

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nafcillin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Piperacillin-tazobactam

explanation.summary: Piperacillin-tazobactam has one of the broadest gram-negative spectra and is used for initial empiric therapy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Piperacillin-tazobactam has broad gram-positive coverage (except MRSA) together with one of the broadest gram-negative coverages, including Enterobacter, Escherichia coli, Klebsiella, Serratia, Proteus, ESBL producers, and Pseudomonas. That breadth is exactly why it is chosen for initial empiric therapy in a septic post-surgical patient. No other listed agent spans gram-positives and Pseudomonas at once.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ampicillin-sulbactam does not cover Pseudomonas or ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Aztreonam treats only aerobic gram-negative bacteria and would leave gram-positive organisms uncovered.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Doxycycline is not effective against Pseudomonas aeruginosa and has limited activity against anaerobes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nafcillin is an antistaphylococcal penicillin with no meaningful gram-negative activity.

questions.topicName: Spectrum of Activity and Indications – 2: β-lactams and 30S Inhibitors

questions.stem: A patient with a complicated intra-abdominal infection is receiving piperacillin-tazobactam, and cultures return a gram-negative bacillus. Which of the following organisms is expected to be covered by this agent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Klebsiella pneumoniae

choices.label: B
choices.text: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mycoplasma pneumoniae

choices.label: D
choices.text: Rickettsia rickettsii

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium

explanation.summary: Piperacillin-tazobactam covers Enterobacteriaceae such as E. coli, Klebsiella, Serratia, and Proteus.
explanation.whyCorrect: Beyond its broad gram-positive coverage, piperacillin-tazobactam covers gram-negative organisms including Enterobacter species, Escherichia coli, Klebsiella, Serratia, and Proteus. Klebsiella pneumoniae therefore falls squarely within its spectrum. This is part of why it is a workhorse empiric agent for intra-abdominal infection.

whyWrongByChoice.B: MRSA is the stated gram-positive exception to piperacillin-tazobactam coverage.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mycoplasma is an atypical pathogen treated with doxycycline, not with a β-lactam.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Rickettsial organisms are treated first-line with doxycycline and are not covered by β-lactams.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus is not within its spectrum; tetracyclines are the class credited with VRE activity.

questions.topicName: Spectrum of Activity and Indications – 2: β-lactams and 30S Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man with a severe skin and soft tissue infection is receiving piperacillin-tazobactam but remains febrile. Blood cultures grow methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. Which of the following best explains the inadequate response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Piperacillin-tazobactam lacks activity against Escherichia coli

choices.label: B
choices.text: Piperacillin-tazobactam lacks activity against Klebsiella species

choices.label: C
choices.text: Piperacillin-tazobactam lacks activity against MRSA

choices.label: D
choices.text: Piperacillin-tazobactam lacks activity against Proteus species

choices.label: E
choices.text: Piperacillin-tazobactam lacks activity against Pseudomonas aeruginosa

explanation.summary: Piperacillin-tazobactam has broad gram-positive coverage except for MRSA.
explanation.whyCorrect: Piperacillin-tazobactam's gram-positive coverage is broad but explicitly excludes MRSA. When MRSA is isolated, an anti-MRSA agent must be used instead of relying on the β-lactam. Its gram-negative reach, by contrast, is one of the broadest available.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Escherichia coli is covered by piperacillin-tazobactam.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Klebsiella is within its gram-negative spectrum.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Proteus is among the gram-negative organisms it covers.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Piperacillin-tazobactam does cover Pseudomonas, which is one of its main advantages.

questions.topicName: Spectrum of Activity and Indications – 2: β-lactams and 30S Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 33-year-old man is hospitalized with bloody diarrhea and bacteremia, and blood cultures grow Campylobacter. Which of the following agents provides coverage of this organism in addition to broad gram-positive and gram-negative coverage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Linezolid

choices.label: B
choices.text: Nafcillin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oral vancomycin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oxacillin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Piperacillin-tazobactam

explanation.summary: Piperacillin-tazobactam's broad spectrum includes Pseudomonas and Campylobacter.
explanation.whyCorrect: Piperacillin-tazobactam has broad gram-positive coverage (except MRSA) and very broad gram-negative coverage that includes Pseudomonas and Campylobacter. That breadth makes it suitable for initial empiric therapy in a septic patient before the organism is known. The other options are gram-positive agents or narrow penicillins.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Linezolid is a gram-positive agent and would not treat a gram-negative enteric organism.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Nafcillin is an antistaphylococcal penicillin and is not effective against many gram-negative bacteria.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Oral vancomycin is not absorbed, works only in the gut lumen, and has no gram-negative activity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Oxacillin is an antistaphylococcal penicillin aimed at gram-positive cocci, not enteric gram-negative rods.

questions.topicName: Spectrum of Activity and Indications – 2: β-lactams and 30S Inhibitors

questions.stem: Blood cultures from a 66-year-old woman with pyelonephritis grow an extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL)-producing Klebsiella pneumoniae. Which of the following agents is the most reliable treatment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Linezolid

choices.label: B
choices.text: Meropenem

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nafcillin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Penicillin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vancomycin

explanation.summary: Carbapenems are the most reliable treatment for ESBL-producing bacteria.
explanation.whyCorrect: Carbapenems are considered the most reliable treatment for infections caused by extended-spectrum β-lactamase producing organisms. Their broad-spectrum activity and stability against β-lactamase enzymes is what preserves activity when other β-lactams are degraded. Meropenem is the only carbapenem among the options.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Linezolid covers gram-positive organisms and has no activity against a gram-negative bacillus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nafcillin is an antistaphylococcal penicillin and is not effective against gram-negative bacteria.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Penicillin is readily degraded by β-lactamases and lacks the needed gram-negative spectrum.
